nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A, Paper 1F, code 4MA1 1F. This is the Foundation tier, for grades 5 to 1. It lasts two hours, has 100 marks, and is 50 percent of the qualification. You may use a calculator, and a formula sheet is printed in the paper. Paper 2F is the same length and covers the same content. Each branch is one question style: read the question, find the key words, plan, work it out, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft: needs review by a maths teacher. (Source: spec pages 5, 10 and 41.)

children.note: Short questions worth one or two marks, mostly on number: place value, rounding, fractions, percentages, powers and standard form. They test assessment objective 1, number and algebra, and often come early in the paper. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)

Read the whole question slowly, twice. In 2025 many students wrote a number that did not use the digits given, because they had not read the question properly. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1F report page 3.)

Underline the words that say what form the answer takes: nearest ten, nearest thousand, simplest form, standard form, or as a fraction. In 2024 some students wrote tenths when the question asked for tens. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 3.)
Name the one skill it needs: rounding, fractions, percentages, or powers. If you use the calculator, decide where the brackets go before you type. (Source: spec page 14, using a calculator.)
Write down what you type, then write the full calculator display. Round only at the end, and only if the question asks. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Not reading the question, for example giving a number that does not use the digits given. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 3.
Mixing up place values, such as tenths and tens. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 3.
Doing a sum in the wrong order, or typing it into the calculator without brackets. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 4, and June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Standard form not finished: 520 times 10 to the power 6 is not standard form. The first number must be from 1 up to 10. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 9.
Powers with brackets: forgetting to apply the power to the number in front as well as the letters. June 2025 Paper 1F report pages 8 and 9.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What does a number in standard form look like? Answer: A number from 1 up to but not including 10, times 10 to a whole-number power. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)
Ask: Round 173 626 to the nearest thousand. Answer: 174 000. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)
Ask: How is nearest ten different from tenths? Answer: Nearest ten is a whole number ending in zero. Tenths is the first place after the decimal point. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)
Ask: When do you round in a calculator question? Answer: Only at the end. Write the full display first. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)
Ask: Is 9 a prime number? Answer: No. 9 is 3 times 3, so it has more than two factors. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)

A real-life problem, often about money, percentages, ratio, units or area. You need several steps. These are usually worth 3 to 5 marks. Problem solving is about a quarter of the Foundation marks. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Read it all before you start. In 2024 some students forgot that there were five packs of butter, not one, and lost two marks. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 5.)
Underline every number with its unit. Circle words such as each, total, left over, increase, decrease, profit and normal price. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 6.)
Write the steps as a short list first: find this, then that, then the answer. Change units first, for example kilograms to grams. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 5.)
Put each step on its own line with a short label, such as cost of two calculators. Keep full calculator values until the end. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 5.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Reverse percentage: if 198 is 72 percent of the normal price, divide 198 by 0.72. Do not add 28 percent. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 9, and June 2024 Paper 1F report page 7.
Missing the last step, for example finding 12 percent but not taking it away. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 6.
Adding when you should multiply, as when counting boxes that fit in a crate. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 5.
Rounding the wrong way: if you need 14.25 tins of paint, you must buy 15. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 7.
Percentage profit: divide the profit by the cost, not by the money taken in. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 8.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many grams are in a kilogram? Answer: 1000 grams. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Ask: A price goes down by 12 percent. What do you multiply by? Answer: 0.88, because 100 minus 12 is 88. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Ask: After a 28 percent cut the price is 198. How do you find the old price? Answer: Divide 198 by 0.72. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Ask: You need 14.25 tins of paint. How many do you buy? Answer: Fifteen. Round up when you buy enough to cover something. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Ask: What should each line of working show? Answer: One step, with a short label so the examiner can follow it. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)

Algebra questions ask you to simplify, expand, factorise, solve an equation, find an nth term, or change the subject of a formula. Each part is usually worth 1 to 3 marks. They test assessment objective 1. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Listen for the action word: simplify, expand, factorise, solve, or make something the subject. Each one asks for a different kind of answer. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1F report page 7.)
Look for the words show clear algebraic working. If you see them, a right answer found by trial and improvement gets no marks. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 8.)
For an equation, plan the order: clear any fraction, expand the brackets, letters on one side and numbers on the other, then divide. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1F report page 9.)
Do one step per line. When a term moves to the other side, change its sign. Take extra care with negative numbers. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 8.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Not knowing what factorise means: put it into brackets, with the common factor outside. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 7.
Sign errors when moving a term, for example adding 11 when you should take it away. June 2024 Paper 1F report pages 4 and 8.
Not clearing a fraction correctly before expanding the brackets. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 9.
Mistakes with negative numbers, such as negative 8 m plus 5 m. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 8.
Writing an nth term as an equation, such as n equals 3 n minus 2. Just write 3 n minus 2. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 6.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What does expand mean? Answer: Multiply out the brackets. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Ask: What does factorise mean? Answer: The opposite of expand: put it back into brackets. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Ask: Solve 6 x equals 42. Answer: x equals 7. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Ask: Plus 11 moves to the other side. What does it become? Answer: Minus 11. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Ask: The question says show clear algebraic working. Can you use trial and improvement? Answer: No. It gets no marks. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)

Some questions give you the answer and ask you to show that it is true. Others say show your working clearly. In both, the working earns the marks, not the final answer. Mathematical reasoning is about 15 percent of the Foundation marks. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Listen for show that, or show your working clearly. These words mean an answer on its own will score nothing. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 7.)
Underline the answer you have to reach. Your last line must match it exactly. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.)
List every step the examiner must see. For fractions: change to improper fractions, write them with a common denominator, then subtract. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.)
Write each step in full, even the easy ones. Write 5625 times 0.24, not just 24 percent of 5625. Finish on the given answer. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
An answer only, from the calculator, when the question said show your working. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 7.
Skipping a step in a show that question, such as the fractions with a common denominator. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.
Not finishing: the working must end on the given answer. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.
Writing 24 percent times 5625, which is not a method. Write 5625 times 0.24. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Two methods with the wrong one on the answer line, which scores zero. This was a question shared by Papers 1F and 1H. June 2025 Paper 1H report page 3.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: In a show that question, do you already know the answer? Answer: Yes. You must show every step that gets you there. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Ask: Does a calculator answer with no working score marks? Answer: No, not when the question asks for working. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Ask: How do you write 7 percent of 4000 as a method? Answer: 4000 times 0.07. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Ask: What must your last line do? Answer: Match the given answer exactly. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Ask: You tried two methods. What do you do? Answer: Choose one and cross out the other, so only one answer is left. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)

Questions on angles, polygons, circles, area, volume, Pythagoras, trigonometry, transformations, and constructions with ruler and compasses. They test assessment objective 2, shape, space and measures. A question is usually worth 1 to 4 marks. Bring a ruler, compasses, a protractor and a sharp pencil. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Diagrams are not drawn to scale unless the question says so. Do not measure them; work the answer out. (Source: spec page 10.)
Underline words such as construct, interior, exterior, radius, diameter, area, circumference and volume. Check which length or angle you must find. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.)

Mark every fact on the diagram in the right place. Choose your tool: an angle fact, a formula from the formula sheet on page 2, Pythagoras, or trigonometry. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1F report page 11.)
Write the formula, put in the numbers, then calculate. In a construction, leave all your compass arcs showing and draw the final line. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Drawing without compass arcs, or leaving arcs but no line. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 5, and June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.
Not using the formula sheet, for example for the area of a trapezium. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 11.
Pythagoras: adding the squares when finding a shorter side, where you must subtract. June 2024 Paper 1F report pages 6 and 9.
Polygons: finding the interior angle and then getting stuck. Use the exterior angle and 360 degrees. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 8.
Mixing up the circumference and the area of a circle. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What do the exterior angles of any polygon add up to? Answer: 360 degrees. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Ask: What do the angles in a quadrilateral add up to? Answer: 360 degrees. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Ask: Name the formulas on the Foundation formula sheet. Answer: Area of a trapezium, volume of a prism, and the volume and curved surface area of a cylinder. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Ask: In a construction, what must you leave on the page? Answer: All your compass arcs, and the finished line. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Ask: What is a tangent to a circle? Answer: A straight line that touches the circle at one point. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)

Graph questions ask you to complete a table of values, plot points, draw a line, read values, or use coordinates. Graphs are part of assessment objective 1, number and algebra. A graph question is usually worth 2 to 4 marks. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Listen for the equation of the line and the range of x values, for example from negative 2 up to 3. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 6.)
Underline complete the table, draw the graph, and the x values. Your line must cover that whole range. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 6.)
Work out every y value in the table first. For a straight line, the y values go up or down by the same amount each time. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1F report page 4.)
Plot each point with a small neat cross: across first, then up. Join the points with one ruled line across the whole range. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Plotting the points but not drawing the line. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 4, and June 2024 Paper 1F report page 6.
Line too short: not drawn across the full range of x values. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 6.
Three or four wrong values in the table. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 4.
Coordinates the wrong way round. x comes first, then y. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.
Misreading a scale by not counting the divisions between the numbers. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: In the point 3 comma 5, which number is x? Answer: 3. Go across first, then up. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Ask: How do you join the points of a straight-line graph? Answer: With one ruled line through all the points. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Ask: How far should the line go? Answer: Across the whole range of x values in the question. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Ask: Before you read a scale, what do you count? Answer: The small divisions between the numbers. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Ask: In a table for a straight line, how do the y values change? Answer: By the same amount each time. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)

These questions use tables, charts, averages, probability, Venn diagrams and sets. They test assessment objective 3, handling data. A question is usually worth 1 to 4 marks. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Find out what the table shows. Which column is the data, and which is the frequency, meaning how many times? (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 5.)
Underline mean, median, mode, range, estimate or probability, and the group the question is about. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.)

For a mean from a table: multiply each value by its frequency, add them up, then divide by the total frequency. For grouped data, use the middle of each group. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1F report page 8.)
Show each multiplication. Write a probability as a fraction, decimal or percentage, never as a ratio. Check it is between 0 and 1. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 5.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Estimated mean: dividing by the number of groups instead of the total frequency. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 8.
Mean from a table: dividing by the sum of the data instead of the sum of the frequencies. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 5.
Writing a probability as a ratio, such as 10 to 29. It gets no marks. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 5.
Using the wrong total for a probability from a two-way table. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.
Sharing what is left of a probability wrongly: one share and two shares means dividing by 3, not by 2. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 7.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What do the probabilities of all the outcomes add up to? Answer: 1. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Ask: Can a probability be 1.2? Answer: No. A probability is always from 0 to 1. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Ask: How should you write a probability? Answer: As a fraction, decimal or percentage, not as a ratio. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Ask: For grouped data, which value do you use for each group? Answer: The middle value of the group. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Ask: For a mean from a frequency table, what do you divide by? Answer: The total frequency. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)

Some questions ask you to give a reason or explain. In geometry you must name the angle fact you used. Other questions ask you to explain a pattern, or what is wrong with some working. A reason is usually worth 1 mark. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec page 21.)
Listen for give a reason, explain, or give a reason for your answer. These need words as well as numbers. (Source: June 2024 Paper 1F report page 4.)
Underline what the reason is about, for example angle x, or the next term in a sequence. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1F report page 4.)
Choose the exact fact, using the standard words, such as angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees. (Source: spec page 21.)
Write one clear sentence with the key words. Add the number or the correct answer too, if it helps. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Using the wrong words, such as angles in a circle, instead of angles around a point add up to 360 degrees. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 4.
A pattern explanation that does not say what changes each time, such as add 4 each time. June 2025 Paper 1F report page 4.
Vague answers, such as they did not use BIDMAS, instead of the exact mistake. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.
Probability: not saying that a probability can never be more than 1. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 3.
Sets: muddled statements, or not knowing the empty set symbol. June 2024 Paper 1F report page 8.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What do angles on a straight line add up to? Answer: 180 degrees. (Source: spec page 21.)
Ask: What do angles around a point add up to? Answer: 360 degrees. (Source: spec page 21.)
Ask: What do the angles in a triangle add up to? Answer: 180 degrees. (Source: spec page 21.)
Ask: What is special about the base angles of an isosceles triangle? Answer: They are equal. (Source: spec page 21.)
Ask: A negative number times a negative number gives what? Answer: A positive number. (Source: spec page 21.)

nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A, Paper 2F, code 4MA1 2F. This is the Foundation tier, for grades 5 to 1. It lasts two hours, has 100 marks, and is 50 percent of the qualification. You may use a calculator, and a formula sheet is printed in the paper. Paper 2F covers the same Foundation content as Paper 1F; the spec does not split topics between the two papers. About 40 percent of the questions are aimed at grades 5 and 4 and are shared with Paper 2H, so the last questions on Paper 2F are often the hardest. Each branch is one question style: read the question, find the key words, plan, work it out, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft: needs review by a maths teacher. (Source: spec page 5, spec page 6, spec page 10 and spec page 41.)

children.note: Short questions worth one or two marks, mostly on number: place value, rounding, fractions, odd and even numbers, and calculator work. They test assessment objective 1, number and algebra. In June 2025 they came at the start of Paper 2F. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)
Read the whole question slowly, twice. The examiners said some students did not read the question properly, and answered a different question. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 3.)

Underline the words that say what form the answer takes: in words, nearest thousand, mixed number, as a fraction, or write down all the figures on your calculator display. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.)
Name the one skill it needs. For a calculator question, decide where the brackets go before you type, so the calculator does the sum in the right order. (Source: spec page 14.)
Write the full calculator display first. Round only at the end, and only if the question asks. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Rounding 173 626 to the nearest thousand as 173 000. The 6 in the hundreds place means you round up to 174 000. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 3.
Mixing up place values, such as circling hundredths when the 7 was worth hundreds. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 3.
Typing a fraction calculation into the calculator without brackets, so the order of operations is wrong. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Over-rounding when the question asked for all the figures on the calculator display. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Missing a number from a list, such as leaving out 1 or 9 from the odd numbers up to 9. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Round 173 626 to the nearest thousand. Answer: 174 000. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)
Ask: What is the place value of the 7 in 406 752? Answer: Seven hundred, so the 7 is in the hundreds column. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)
Ask: Write 0.3 as a fraction. Answer: Three tenths. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)
Ask: List the positive odd numbers up to and including 9. Answer: 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)
Ask: A question says write down all the figures on your calculator display. Do you round? Answer: No. Write every figure you see. (Source: spec pages 11 to 14.)

A real-life problem, often about money, units, recipes, percentages, ratio or interest. You need several steps. In June 2025 these were worth 2 to 4 marks each. The examiners said everyday problems and percentages were hard for many students. Problem solving is about a quarter of the Foundation marks. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Read it all before you start. In the car factory question, some students did not see that they had to find 24 percent of the cars. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 3.)
Underline every number with its unit. Change units first: 2 litres is 2000 millilitres, not 200. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.)

Write the steps as a short list first. For the cupcakes: find the cost of two cupcakes, take it away from the total, then share what is left between five doughnuts. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.)
Put each step on its own line with a short label. Keep full values until the end. Do not round a scale factor such as 4.5. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 7.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Dividing the wrong way round, such as 3 divided by 2.25 instead of 2.25 divided by 3. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.
Leaving a part answer such as 11.11 cups. Only 11 whole cups can be filled, so work with 11. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.
Finding 24 percent by dividing by 24 and then multiplying by 100. Multiply by 0.24 instead. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Rounding a scale factor of 4.5 to 5 before using it. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 7.
Compound interest worked as simple interest, or using 1.7 instead of 1.07 for a 7 percent rise. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 9.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many millilitres are in 2 litres? Answer: 2000 millilitres. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Ask: Interest of 7 percent a year is added for 3 years. What do you multiply by? Answer: 1.07, three times. That is 1.07 cubed. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Ask: How do you find 24 percent of 5625? Answer: Multiply 5625 by 0.24. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Ask: Share 240 in the ratio 3 to 4 to 5. What is one part worth? Answer: 20, because 3 plus 4 plus 5 is 12, and 240 divided by 12 is 20. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)
Ask: A recipe for 4 people is made for 18. What is the scale factor? Answer: 4.5. Keep it as 4.5; do not round it. (Source: spec page 43; spec page 9.)

Algebra questions ask you to simplify, collect like terms, write a formula, change the subject, solve simultaneous equations, or solve an inequality. Each part is usually worth 1 to 3 marks. They test assessment objective 1. In June 2025, the later algebra questions on Paper 2F were left blank by many students. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Listen for the action word: simplify, solve, write a formula, or make y the subject. Each one asks for a different kind of answer. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.)
Notice sum and product. d plus d plus d plus d is 4 d, a sum. w times w times w times w times w is w to the power 5, a product. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 3.)
For simultaneous equations, plan to make the number in front of one letter the same in both equations, then subtract or add to get rid of that letter. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 9.)
Do one step per line, and write each step down. Students who wrote only the answer when changing the subject usually got it wrong. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Collecting like terms: adding the y terms when one of them should be taken away. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 3.
Changing the subject: taking d away from w, when you must add d to both sides. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Writing a formula: T equals b plus p, instead of T equals 12 b plus 3 p. Each box holds 12 and each packet holds 3. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Simultaneous equations: not multiplying every term, or adding when you should subtract. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 9.
Inequality: dividing by a negative number and not turning the sign round. June 2025 Paper 2H report page 6.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Simplify d plus d plus d plus d. Answer: 4 d. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Ask: Make y the subject of w equals 3 y minus d. Answer: y equals w plus d, all divided by 3. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Ask: Solve 6 x equals 42. Answer: x equals 7. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Ask: In simultaneous equations, why do you make the numbers in front of x match? Answer: So you can subtract and get rid of x. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)
Ask: You divide both sides of an inequality by negative 5. What happens to the sign? Answer: It turns round. Less than becomes greater than. (Source: spec pages 15 to 17.)

Some questions give you the answer and ask you to show that it is true. Others need clear working to earn method marks. In both, the working earns the marks, not the final answer. Mathematical reasoning is about 15 percent of the Foundation marks. In June 2025 the fractions show that question on Paper 2F was worth 3 marks. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Listen for show that. It means you already know the answer, and the marks are for every step that gets you there. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.)
Underline the answer you have to reach. Your last line must match it exactly. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.)
For mixed numbers: change both to improper fractions, write them with a common denominator, then subtract. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2H report page 4.)
Write each step in full, even the easy ones. Write 5625 times 0.24, not 24 percent times 5625. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Leaving out the step with the common denominator in a fractions show that question. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.
Not finishing: the working must end on the given answer. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.
Writing 24 percent times 5625, which is not a method. Write 5625 times 0.24. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Writing 1 plus 7 percent in a calculation. Write 1 plus 0.07 instead, so the method mark can be given. June 2025 Paper 2H report page 5.
Trial and improvement, or random combining of numbers, which cannot gain method marks. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 11.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: In a show that question, do you already know the answer? Answer: Yes. You must show every step that gets you there. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Ask: How do you write 7 percent of 4000 as a method? Answer: 4000 times 0.07. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Ask: What is 3 and 1 seventh as an improper fraction? Answer: 22 sevenths. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Ask: What must your last line do? Answer: Match the given answer exactly. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)
Ask: Simultaneous equations: do you get marks for just writing the answers? Answer: No. You must show the algebra. (Source: spec page 9; spec page 43.)

Questions on angles, circles, bearings, enlargement, similar shapes, Pythagoras, and constructions with ruler and compasses. They test assessment objective 2, shape, space and measures. In June 2025 they were worth 2 to 5 marks each on Paper 2F, and the examiners said Pythagoras was a striking weakness. Bring a ruler, compasses, a protractor and a sharp, dark pencil. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Diagrams are not drawn accurately unless the question says so. Do not measure them. Students who measured the bearing got no marks. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 7.)
Underline words such as circumference, area, bearing of A from B, scale factor, centre, and perpendicular bisector. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.)

Mark each fact on the diagram in the right place. For similar shapes, find the scale factor by dividing, then multiply. Do not add the difference between sides. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.)
Write the formula, put in the numbers, then calculate. In a construction, leave both pairs of arcs showing, and draw the line through them. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Writing a correct angle on the diagram, but in the wrong position. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.
Using the area formula for a circle when the question needs the circumference. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 6.
Measuring a bearing on a diagram that is not drawn accurately. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 7.
Drawing the arcs for a perpendicular bisector but not the line, or arcs too close to use. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 8.
Pythagoras: using it in a triangle with no right angle, or forgetting the last subtraction. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 11.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What is the formula for the circumference of a circle? Answer: Pi times the diameter, or 2 times pi times the radius. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Ask: The bearing of B from A is 073 degrees. What is the bearing of A from B? Answer: 253 degrees. Add 180. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Ask: Two sides that match are 4 and 10. What is the scale factor? Answer: 2.5, because 10 divided by 4 is 2.5. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Ask: When can you use Pythagoras? Answer: Only in a right-angled triangle. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)
Ask: In a construction, what must you leave on the page? Answer: All your compass arcs, and the finished line. (Source: spec pages 19 to 23.)

Graph questions ask you to read a number line, use coordinates, find a midpoint, or give the inequalities that describe a region on a grid. Graphs are part of assessment objective 1, number and algebra. In June 2025 the region question on Paper 2F was worth 3 marks, and very few students scored. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Count the small divisions between the numbers on a number line or scale before you read it. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.)
Underline coordinates, midpoint, region, and inequalities. Each asks for a different kind of answer. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 10.)
For a midpoint, add the two x values and halve, then add the two y values and halve. Do not subtract. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.)
For a region, write one inequality for each line around it, such as x is greater than or equal to 2. Check the sign with a point inside the region. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 10.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Misreading a number line by not counting the divisions between the numbers. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.
Coordinates the wrong way round. x comes first, then y. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.
Finding a midpoint by subtracting the coordinates instead of adding them. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 4.
Listing the corner points of a region instead of writing inequalities. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 10.
Inequality signs the wrong way round, so they describe the outside of the region. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 10.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: In the point 3 comma 5, which number is x? Answer: 3. Go across first, then up. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Ask: What is the midpoint of 2 comma 4 and 6 comma 8? Answer: 4 comma 6. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Ask: Before you read a scale, what do you count? Answer: The small divisions between the numbers. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Ask: A region is to the right of the line x equals 2. What inequality is that? Answer: x is greater than or equal to 2. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)
Ask: How can you check an inequality for a region? Answer: Pick a point inside the region and see if it fits. (Source: spec pages 17 to 18.)

These questions use tally charts, bar charts, two-way tables, averages and probability. They test assessment objective 3, handling data. In June 2025 they were worth 2 to 3 marks each on Paper 2F, and the last question on the paper was probability. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Find out which group the question is about. Chosen from those playing cricket means you only count the children who play cricket. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.)
Underline range, median, mode, mean or probability. Do not mix them up. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2H report page 3.)
For a missing number of counters: the red and blue probability is 1 take away 4 ninths, which is 5 ninths. So 45 counters are 5 ninths of the bag. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 11.)
Show each step. Write a probability as a fraction, decimal or percentage. Label every bar on a bar chart. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 3.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Bars on a bar chart not labelled. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 3.
Using the wrong total for a probability from a two-way table. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.
Writing the median, 7.5, on a card. The median is halfway between the two middle cards. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 7.
Finding 4 ninths of 45 to get the number of orange counters. This got no marks. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 11.
Giving the total number of counters, 81, when the question asked for the orange counters, 36. June 2025 Paper 2H report page 7.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What do the probabilities of all the outcomes add up to? Answer: 1. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Ask: What is the range? Answer: The biggest value take away the smallest. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Ask: What is the mode? Answer: The value that appears most often. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Ask: Six numbers in order. Where is the median? Answer: Halfway between the third and the fourth number. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)
Ask: The probability of orange is 4 ninths. What is the probability of not orange? Answer: 5 ninths. (Source: spec pages 24 to 25.)

Some questions ask you to explain what is wrong with some working, or to describe a transformation in words. A reason is usually worth 1 mark. Describing a rotation fully was worth 3 marks on Paper 2F in June 2025. Our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to check. (Source: spec page 21; spec page 23.)
Listen for explain what is wrong, or describe fully the single transformation. These need words as well as numbers. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.)
Underline single and fully. Single means one transformation only. Fully means give every detail. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2H report page 3.)
For a rotation, plan three facts: the word rotation, the angle and direction, and the centre as coordinates. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 7.)
Write one clear sentence naming the exact mistake. Writing the correct answer as well can earn the mark. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Vague answers, such as they did not use BIDMAS, instead of the exact mistake. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.
Not saying the key fact: a negative times a negative gives a positive. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 5.
Describing a rotation without all three facts: rotation, angle, and centre. June 2025 Paper 2F report page 7.
Giving more than one transformation when the question asks for a single one. June 2025 Paper 2H report page 3.
Writing turn instead of rotation, or writing the centre as a vector instead of coordinates. June 2025 Paper 2H report page 3.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: A negative number times a negative number gives what? Answer: A positive number. (Source: spec page 21; spec page 23.)
Ask: What three facts describe a rotation? Answer: The word rotation, the angle and direction, and the centre. (Source: spec page 21; spec page 23.)
Ask: Should you say turn or rotation? Answer: Rotation. (Source: spec page 21; spec page 23.)
Ask: How do you write the centre of a rotation? Answer: As coordinates, such as 5 comma 5. (Source: spec page 21; spec page 23.)
Ask: Is they forgot BIDMAS a good explanation? Answer: No. Say the exact mistake. (Source: spec page 21; spec page 23.)
